project.objective: When and where did Victoriana Vasquez, daughter of Remigio Vasquez and Bernarda Sandoval, marry Jose Cleofas Gutierrez?

researcher_profile.narration_guidance: Plain language for someone who has never done genealogy. No identifiers, file names, tool names or field names. Never write GPS, proof, proved or exhaustive: say genealogy standards; call an answer a conclusion when it is well established and a finding otherwise; say what we searched and what we could not reach. Do not describe your own instructions or checks. Do not narrate between actions; report once when the step is done: what was found, in one paragraph, and what happens next in one sentence.

questions.question: When and where did Victoriana Vasquez, daughter of Remigio Vasquez and Bernarda Sandoval, marry Jose Cleofas Gutierrez?
questions.rationale: This is the project's single-fact objective — the date and place of one marriage event. No sources are attached to any person in the tree, and no prior research exists. Marriage records for Hispanic families in the relevant region are typically found in Catholic parish registers and civil registration records, both of which are searchable by bride and groom name. Establishing the date and place of this marriage is the entire scope of the project.

items.rationale: New Mexico, Marriages, 1751-1918 is name-searchable (personCount 251,436) and covers the Spanish colonial, Mexican territorial, and US Territorial periods — the most likely window for a Hispanic New Mexico family. Under the Mexico Naming Customs wiki (fetched this session), Victoriana's full compound surname is Vasquez Sandoval (paternal Vasquez from father Remigio, maternal Sandoval from mother Bernarda); records will list her as 'Vasquez' or 'Vasquez Sandoval.' Search for her under both forms as bride and for Jose Cleofas Gutierrez as groom. The bride retains her maiden surname in Catholic and civil records.

New Mexico, County Marriages, 1885-1954 is name-searchable (personCount 162,523) and covers county-level civil marriage licenses and bonds through early statehood (New Mexico achieved statehood 6 January 1912). This collection partially overlaps chronologically with item 1 but draws on county courthouse civil-registration sources distinct from the indexed church registers. Both collections must be searched independently because a Catholic church marriage and a civil bond/license are separate instruments and may index differently.

US Federal Census records (1880, 1900, 1910, 1920, 1930) are name-searchable on FamilySearch. The 1900 schedule records the number of years each person has been married and the year of immigration if foreign-born; the 1910 schedule records years of present marriage; both bracket the marriage date directly. Census records also place the couple and child Silveria Gutierrez in a specific county, identifying the county whose records to prioritize when browsing the unindexed Catholic registers (item 5). Also search the New Mexico, Territorial Census, 1885 (name-searchable, personCount 59,040) on FamilySearch for early placement. Search under both 'Vasquez' and 'Gutierrez' surnames for either spouse.

FAN item: New Mexico, Births and Christenings, 1726-1918 is name-searchable (personCount 764,129). Searching for the baptism of daughter Silveria Gutierrez would name her parents — Victoriana Vasquez and Jose Cleofas Gutierrez — and typically records the parents' parish of residence, often their marriage date and parish. The child's baptism is the record most likely to state directly when and where the parents married, since the officiating priest frequently asked for that information. Also search for Victoriana's own baptism record under 'Vasquez Sandoval,' which would establish her home parish — often the same parish where the marriage took place.

New Mexico, Catholic Church Records, 1701-1956 is browse-only (personCount 0) — the digitized Catholic parish registers are not name-indexed and must be browsed by parish. This item should follow census and child-baptism searches (items 3-4), which are expected to narrow the search to a specific county and parish before browsing. Under Catholic practice, the velación (formal nuptial blessing recorded separately from the civil act) and the marriage investigation (informaciones matrimoniales) may appear in registers distinct from the main marriage libro. Browse the marriage books of the identified parish for entries listing Vasquez or Gutierrez.

Ancestry.com holds New Mexico marriage records and US census collections that overlap with items 1-3 and may carry digitized images not visible in the FamilySearch index alone. If FamilySearch name searches on items 1 and 2 yield no result, Ancestry's New Mexico marriage index and its US census collections (which include the 1900 and 1910 schedules with years-married fields) provide an independent search path through a different indexing pipeline. Ancestry also holds the New Mexico Territorial and county marriage bonds that may index slightly different name spellings.
items.skip_reason: Ancestry.com requires a subscription and a user capture; no user was present to click the link and return a PDF during this autonomous run. Three search URLs were generated and logged (log_076, log_077, log_078) for the researcher to execute later. FamilySearch holds equivalent collections (NM County Marriages 1885-1954, and both census years) that search-records can reach without a capture.

items.rationale: Mexico, Chihuahua, Catholic Church Records, 1632-2005 is name-searchable (personCount 11,115,750). Chihuahua is the Mexican state directly bordering New Mexico and is the most geographically plausible state of origin if the family came from Mexico rather than the US territory. If all New Mexico searches are negative, search for the marriage record of Victoriana Vasquez Sandoval and Jose Cleofas Gutierrez in Chihuahua's Catholic registers. Also search Mexico, Chihuahua, Civil Registration, 1861-1997 (name-searchable, personCount 8,411,748) as the civil counterpart — Mexico mandated civil registration beginning 1859-1861. A Chihuahua baptism for either principal would also name their home parish and corroborate a Mexican rather than New Mexican origin.
